subject: religious-studies
topicDisplay: Introduction To Religions Two From The Sl List
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the sociology of religion, Max Weber's account of secularisation links the 'disenchantment of the world' primarily to:
options: The rationalisation brought by science and bureaucracy
The rise of fundamentalist movements
The decline of printed scripture
An increase in private prayer
questions.explain: Weber argued that rationalisation progressively strips the world of magical and sacred explanation, replacing enchantment with calculable, scientific understanding.

questions.q: Emil Fackenheim's theological response to the Holocaust centres on the idea of:
options: A literal return to Temple sacrifice
The denial of the covenant
The abandonment of all Jewish practice
A '614th commandment' not to grant Hitler a posthumous victory
questions.explain: Fackenheim argued that Jews are commanded to survive as Jews and sustain the covenant, lest the destruction of Judaism complete Hitler's aim.

questions.q: Compared with Orthodox Judaism, Reform Judaism is generally characterised by:
options: Rejection of all ethical teaching of the Torah
A belief that the Torah was not divinely inspired at all
Stricter adherence to the totality of halakhah
A more liberal stance, treating much halakhah as non-binding and historically conditioned
questions.explain: Reform Judaism emphasises ethical monotheism and individual autonomy, regarding ritual law as evolving and not uniformly obligatory, in contrast to Orthodoxy's binding halakhah.

questions.q: The Second Noble Truth (samudaya) identifies the origin of suffering as:
options: Ignorance of scripture
Physical illness alone
The actions of malevolent deities
Craving or attachment (tanha)
questions.explain: The Second Noble Truth locates the cause of dukkha in tanha, the thirst or craving that binds beings to the cycle of rebirth.

questions.q: The Mool Mantar, which opens the Guru Granth Sahib, primarily affirms:
options: The doctrine of many gods
The superiority of the Khalsa over other Sikhs
The necessity of caste distinctions
The oneness of God (Ik Onkar) and key divine attributes
questions.explain: The Mool Mantar begins with 'Ik Onkar', declaring God as one, timeless, self-existent and beyond fear or enmity, summarising core Sikh belief.

questions.q: In mainstream Christian theology, the doctrine of the Trinity holds that God is:
options: One God who became human only at the incarnation
A single person who appears in three successive modes
One substance (ousia) in three persons (hypostases)
Three separate gods working in harmony
questions.explain: Trinitarian orthodoxy, codified at Nicaea and Constantinople, affirms one divine essence subsisting in three co-equal, co-eternal persons, rejecting both tritheism and modalism.

questions.q: In Sikh teaching, the practice of sewa (selfless service) and langar (the communal kitchen) chiefly express:
options: A requirement only for the Gurus
Equality of all people and devotion expressed through service
The earning of merit to escape rebirth alone
Ritual purity laws separating communities
questions.explain: Langar and sewa embody the Sikh rejection of caste and social hierarchy, enacting human equality and devotion to God through humble service to others.

questions.q: In Sikhism, regarding the Guru Granth Sahib as the 'living Guru' means that:
options: Only the Ten Gurus may interpret it
It replaces belief in one God
The scripture itself holds the eternal authority of Guruship after Guru Gobind Singh
A human Guru continues to be appointed in each generation
questions.explain: Guru Gobind Singh declared the scripture the eternal Guru, so the Guru Granth Sahib carries living spiritual authority and is treated with the reverence due a Guru.

questions.q: The concept of dharma in Hinduism is best understood as:
options: The illusion masking ultimate reality
The desire that fuels rebirth
The final dissolution of the self
Cosmic and social duty, order and righteousness
questions.explain: Dharma denotes the moral and cosmic order and one's righteous duty, often shaped by varna and ashrama, and is one of the purusharthas (aims of life).

questions.q: Liberation theology, associated with figures such as Gustavo Gutiérrez, is best characterised by its emphasis on:
options: The primacy of monastic contemplation
Literal biblical inerrancy
A 'preferential option for the poor' and structural justice
Withdrawal from political engagement
questions.explain: Liberation theology reads the Gospel as a call to confront social and economic oppression, prioritising the liberation of the marginalised.

questions.q: Within Islam, the concept of Tawhid most precisely refers to:
options: The succession of the caliphs
The absolute oneness and indivisible unity of God
The pilgrimage to Mecca
The five daily prayers
questions.explain: Tawhid is the foundational affirmation of God's absolute unity and uniqueness, and its opposite, shirk (associating partners with God), is regarded as the gravest sin.

questions.q: Modern political Zionism, as articulated by Theodor Herzl, was primarily a response to:
options: The destruction of the Second Temple
Disagreement over kosher law
A theological dispute over the Messiah's identity
Persistent European antisemitism and the desire for a Jewish homeland
questions.explain: Herzl's 'Der Judenstaat' framed a national homeland as a response to entrenched antisemitism, though Zionism's relationship to traditional messianic expectation remains debated.

questions.q: The Bhagavad Gita's teaching of karma yoga primarily advocates:
options: Renouncing all action to attain liberation
Ritual sacrifice as the sole path to the divine
Withdrawal into silent meditation alone
Performing one's duty without attachment to the fruits of action
questions.explain: Krishna instructs Arjuna to act in accordance with his dharma while relinquishing attachment to outcomes, presenting selfless action as a path to liberation.

questions.q: The Three Marks of Existence (tilakkhana) in Buddhism are:
options: Body, speech and mind
Anicca, dukkha and anatta
Greed, hatred and delusion
Birth, ageing and death
questions.explain: The three marks are impermanence (anicca), unsatisfactoriness/suffering (dukkha) and not-self (anatta), characterising all conditioned phenomena.

questions.q: The Khalsa, established by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699, is best described as:
options: A purely ceremonial title with no obligations
A council that elects future Gurus
A monastic order requiring celibacy
The community of initiated Sikhs committed to the discipline and the Five Ks
questions.explain: The Khalsa is the order of committed, initiated (amritdhari) Sikhs who uphold a code of conduct (rahit) including the Five Ks, blending spiritual devotion with moral discipline.

questions.q: In Islamic thought, the Sunnah refers to:
options: The example, sayings and practice of the Prophet Muhammad
The mystical poetry of the Sufi orders
The legal rulings of the four Sunni schools only
The literal text revealed in the Qur'an
questions.explain: The Sunnah is the normative model of Muhammad's words and deeds, recorded in hadith, and stands as the second source of authority after the Qur'an.

questions.q: A key doctrinal emphasis distinguishing Mahayana from Theravada Buddhism is:
options: Rejection of the Buddha's authority
The denial of karma
The abolition of monastic life
The bodhisattva ideal of compassionate postponement of nirvana for all beings
questions.explain: Mahayana elevates the bodhisattva who vows to liberate all sentient beings, alongside concepts such as sunyata, whereas Theravada emphasises the arhat's individual liberation.

questions.q: In Hindu thought, moksha refers to:
options: Devotion to a single chosen deity
Liberation from the cycle of samsara
The performance of correct ritual sacrifice
The accumulation of good karma for a better rebirth
questions.explain: Moksha is release from the round of birth, death and rebirth (samsara), the ultimate spiritual goal among the four aims of human life.

questions.q: The term 'Tenakh' is an acronym denoting the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible, namely:
options: Mishnah, Gemara and Halakhah
Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim
Gospels, Prophets and Psalms
Torah, Talmud and Midrash
questions.explain: Tenakh (TaNaKh) combines Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings), the canonical structure of the Hebrew scriptures.

questions.q: In Christian responses to science, the position that science and religion address fundamentally different questions is most associated with:
options: Strict biblical literalism
Intelligent design theory
Young-earth creationism
Stephen Jay Gould's 'Non-Overlapping Magisteria' (NOMA)
questions.explain: NOMA holds that science covers the empirical realm of fact while religion addresses meaning and value, so the two need not conflict, a model many theologians qualify.

questions.q: In Buddhism, the doctrine of anatta (anatman) teaches that:
options: Only the body is real, the mind illusory
The self merges with Brahman at death
There is an eternal, unchanging soul
There is no fixed, permanent self
questions.explain: Anatta holds that what we call a 'self' is a changing aggregation (the five skandhas) with no permanent essence, distinguishing Buddhism sharply from Hindu atman doctrine.

questions.q: In Islamic doctrine, the Qur'an is traditionally regarded as:
options: The uncreated, literal word of God revealed in Arabic
One scripture among several of equal authority for Muslims
A human commentary on the Torah
A collection of Muhammad's own teachings
questions.explain: Orthodox Islamic belief affirms the Qur'an as the eternal speech of God transmitted verbatim through Muhammad, making its Arabic text inimitable (i'jaz).

questions.q: In post-Holocaust Jewish theology, Richard Rubenstein is best known for arguing that:
options: Suffering always strengthens covenantal faith
The Holocaust was a justified divine punishment
The Holocaust proves God's special protection of Israel
Traditional belief in an omnipotent God of history is no longer tenable
questions.explain: Rubenstein, in 'After Auschwitz', contended that the Shoah challenges belief in a providential God acting in history, a radical response that other thinkers such as Fackenheim resisted.

questions.q: In Judaism, the covenant established at Sinai is best understood as:
options: A reciprocal relationship binding God and Israel through Torah obligation
An unconditional promise requiring nothing of Israel
A purely symbolic ritual with no ethical content
A covenant later annulled by the prophets
questions.explain: The Sinai covenant is mutual: God elects Israel as a people, and Israel binds itself to observe the mitzvot of the Torah, a relationship of obligation and faithfulness.

questions.q: Within the Noble Eightfold Path, 'Right Mindfulness' (samma sati) belongs to which of the three traditional divisions?
options: Panna (wisdom)
Sila (ethical conduct)
Dana (generosity)
Samadhi (mental discipline/meditation)
questions.explain: The Eightfold Path is grouped into wisdom, ethics and meditation; mindfulness and concentration fall under samadhi, the cultivation of disciplined mental states.

questions.q: The Christian claim that God is 'omnibenevolent' is most directly challenged by which theological problem?
options: The problem of evil and suffering
The problem of religious language
The problem of the historical Jesus
The problem of the Eucharist's nature
questions.explain: An all-loving, all-powerful God appears in tension with the existence of gratuitous evil, the central problem addressed by theodicies such as Augustine's and Irenaeus's.

questions.q: The principal theological distinction underlying the Sunni–Shia division concerns:
options: Whether the Qur'an is created or uncreated
The legitimate succession of authority after Muhammad
Whether God is one or many
The direction faced during prayer
questions.explain: Shia Islam holds that leadership rightly passed to Ali and the Imams of the Prophet's household, whereas Sunnis accept the caliphate, a dispute over rightful authority.

questions.q: Among the six orthodox darshanas of Hindu philosophy, the Samkhya school is distinctive for its:
options: Strict monotheism centred on Vishnu
Denial of the authority of the Vedas
Dualism of purusha (consciousness) and prakriti (matter)
Rejection of the concept of liberation
questions.explain: Samkhya posits a fundamental dualism between pure consciousness (purusha) and primal matter (prakriti), and liberation comes through discriminating between the two.

questions.q: In Hinduism, the relationship between atman and Brahman in Advaita Vedanta, as taught by Shankara, is best expressed as:
options: Atman and Brahman are utterly separate
Atman is destroyed at moksha
Brahman is merely a poetic name for the self
Atman is ultimately identical with Brahman
questions.explain: Advaita ('non-dual') Vedanta teaches that the individual self (atman) is ultimately one with the absolute reality (Brahman), and realising this identity is liberation.

questions.q: In Islam, the concept of the ummah refers to:
options: The annual pilgrimage caravan
The legal code of a single madhhab
The ruling political dynasty
The worldwide community of Muslim believers
questions.explain: The ummah is the global community of Muslims united by shared faith, transcending ethnic and national boundaries, a key concept for Islam in the modern world.
